title: IELTS Academic Reading Practice Test 28
instructions: You should spend about 20 minutes on each passage. Answer all questions.

passages.title: Taking It Off the Shelf Yourself
passages.text:
A. Buying food was once a conversation. A customer asked for what they wanted, an assistant fetched it from behind a counter, weighed it, wrapped it and often recorded it against an account. The goods were not accessible, prices were frequently negotiable, and the transaction depended on a relationship between two people who expected to see each other again.

B. Self-service inverted every part of that. Customers were admitted to the stock, given a basket, expected to select without assistance and to pay at a single point on the way out. The labour of fetching, weighing and wrapping transferred to the customer and to the factory, and the assistant who had known what each household bought was replaced by a person operating a till.

C. Packaging was the precondition rather than a consequence. Goods sold loose from sacks and barrels cannot be handled by customers or priced without weighing, so pre-measured sealed units had to exist before the shop could work at all. Once they did, the package became the only thing speaking for the product in the absence of an assistant, which is the origin of most of what packaging now does.

D. The economics that followed were not obvious in advance. Lower labour per sale meant lower prices, lower prices meant higher volume, and higher volume meant better terms from suppliers, which allowed lower prices again. The loop favoured whoever was already largest, and the concentration of food retailing into a small number of very large firms in most high-income countries follows from a mechanism visible from the beginning.

E. The store itself became an instrument once the customer was choosing unaided. Shelf position, floor layout, lighting and the placement of staple goods at the furthest point from the entrance are all decisions about behaviour rather than about storage, and they are tested rather than guessed. A shop arranged for the convenience of shoppers and a shop arranged to maximise what they buy are not the same shop.

F. What has changed most recently is that the same logic has been applied to the customer as data. A store that records who bought what, when and in what combination can price, place and promote by observation rather than by inference, and the loyalty scheme that appears to be a discount is the instrument that collects it. The transaction has become legible to the seller in a way that the counter-and-assistant arrangement, for all its personal knowledge, never made it.

passages.title: The River Will Have Its Room
passages.text:
A river is not a pipe, and most of the damage attributed to floods follows from managing it as though it were. A watercourse and its floodplain are a single system: the channel carries ordinary flow, and the flat land beside it exists because the river has periodically occupied it, depositing the sediment that made the ground fertile enough to attract settlement in the first place. Building on a floodplain is not unlucky. It is building in the part of the river that is used less often.

Engineering responses have historically aimed at containment, and containment moves the problem rather than removing it. Raising banks and straightening channels increases the speed and volume of water leaving a given stretch, which reduces flooding there and increases it downstream, and the response downstream is usually to raise banks in turn. The result is a system in which each reach is protected against the flow the previous reach has accelerated, and in which failure, when it comes, is sudden rather than gradual.

Embankments also create a hazard that unprotected land does not have. Land behind a bank floods rarely, so it is built on densely and its occupants stop expecting water; when the bank is overtopped or breached the water arrives fast, deep and without warning into an area that has forgotten it is a floodplain. Recorded damage per event tends to rise after protection is built, because the protection changed what was there to damage.

Upstream land use matters more than most flood spending acknowledges. Water that soaks into soil, is held by vegetation or is delayed in a wetland does not arrive at once; land that is drained, compacted or paved delivers the same rainfall to the channel in a fraction of the time. Peak flow is a function of timing as much as of quantity, and a catchment that has been systematically drained for agriculture produces higher peaks from unchanged rainfall.

The approach that has gained ground reverses the aim. Rather than moving water away as fast as possible, it slows and stores it: restoring meanders, reconnecting floodplains, planting in headwaters, and accepting inundation on land chosen for the purpose. The measures are often cheaper than concrete for the protection they give, deliver benefits beyond flooding, and are harder to commission because they are distributed, slow to show effect and produce no single visible structure to point at.

Neither approach removes the residual decision, and pretending otherwise is the recurring political failure. Some places cannot be defended at acceptable cost, and the honest response is to say so early enough that people can plan, rather than to maintain defences that will eventually fail and to compensate afterwards. Almost no political system finds it possible to say this, which is why it is usually said by the water instead.

passages.title: Fractions of a Cent
passages.text:
The streaming service resolved a problem that the industry had failed to solve by enforcement. Unauthorised copying had made recorded music effectively free for anyone willing to find it, and a decade of litigation had not changed that; what changed it was a legal service more convenient than the unauthorised one. Convenience, not morality or law, moved the behaviour, which is a lesson the industry has been reluctant to state plainly.

The economics that replaced the old model are not a smaller version of it but a different shape. A recording once generated revenue when a copy was sold, in a transaction complete at the point of purchase. It now generates a fraction of a cent each time it is played, indefinitely, which converts a business of releases into a business of accumulating catalogue and makes the value of a recording depend on how long it keeps being played rather than on how many people wanted it at release.

The distribution of that revenue is where most of the argument sits and it is frequently misdescribed. The service pays out a large share of what it receives, so the complaint that services keep too much is weaker than it sounds; what determines an artist's income is the contract dividing that payment between label and performer, which is a matter of agreements signed under conditions inherited from the era of physical sales. The money is distributed according to who owns the recording, not according to who made it.

The pooling method matters more than most listeners realise. Under the common arrangement, all subscription revenue is combined and divided according to each recording's share of total plays, which means a subscriber's payment goes overwhelmingly to the most-played artists regardless of what that subscriber listened to. An alternative dividing each subscriber's payment among the artists that subscriber actually played has been trialled and shifts money measurably towards smaller and specialist acts.

Discovery has consolidated rather than diversified, contrary to early expectation. The catalogue is effectively unlimited, but attention is not, and recommendation systems trained on aggregate behaviour direct listeners towards what is already popular. The long tail exists and is longer than ever; the proportion of listening it accounts for has not grown as predicted, and placement on a widely followed playlist now functions much as radio programming once did.

Live performance has absorbed what recording no longer provides, with consequences that are unevenly distributed. Touring income has become the principal earning route for most working musicians, which favours those able to travel constantly, disadvantages those who cannot, and makes an activity that is physically demanding and geographically constrained into the foundation of a career that was previously supported by a product requiring neither.
